title: Dominance Signals
description: Territorial behaviors and postures that project authority, power, and high social status.

sections.title: Quick Understanding
sections.content: Dominance signals are behaviors designed to assert authority over an environment and the people in it. They rely heavily on taking up maximum physical space, controlling the flow of conversation, and intentionally forcing others to naturally yield.

sections.title: What It Looks Like
content: Splaying arms widely over the back of an empty chair or across a table.
Using a loud, booming voice to talk over other people.
Deliberately invading another person's personal space.
A terribly firm, crushing handshake, often involving a 'double-hander' dominant grip.
Staring unblinkingly until the other person looks away.

sections.title: What It May Indicate
content: A highly competitive personality actively trying to establish a hierarchy.
Genuine authority and actual status in a specific setting.
Deep insecurity desperately masquerading as power.

sections.title: What It Does NOT Mean
content: Dominant physical behavior does NOT equal actual genuine leadership. Truly great secure leaders often lead perfectly with calm warmth, while insecure bullies lead exclusively with forced dominance.
Expansive posturing definitely does NOT mean they are right; it just means they want to win the argument.

sections.title: Real Life Examples
content: Negotiation: A buyer spreading all of their paperwork deliberately over the entire table, encroaching directly onto your side.
Workplace: A manager standing directly and forcefully over a seated employee's desk while giving feedback.
Social: A person aggressively maintaining intense, unbroken eye contact and refusing entirely to blink.

sections.title: Cluster Analysis
content: Expansive seating + relaxed smile + open hands = Comfortable, actual authority.
Invading space + hard stare + deep frown = Aggressive, intimidating power play.

sections.title: Common Situations
content: High-stakes corporate boardrooms.
Power struggles between competitive peers or siblings.
Hostile legal depositions.

sections.title: Observation Mistakes
sections.content: Mistake: Yielding to unnecessary dominance signals because they naturally feel authoritative. Reality: Many dominance signals are cheap spatial tricks used by deeply insecure people to prevent others from formally challenging them.

sections.title: Practical Observation Tips
content: Notice precisely how space is claimed. Dominant people treat public space as their own private property (e.g., spreading legs wide, leaving their coat on multiple open chairs).
To effectively counter dominance safely, carefully maintain a steady, highly relaxed baseline. Do not match their aggression, but do not shrink your posture either.

sections.title: Red Flags
content: Someone deliberately using physical intimidation (standing far too close) to force a rapid agreement.
Routinely employing the 'bone-crushing' handshake specifically to establish physical superiority right at the start of a meeting.

sections.title: Reality Check
sections.content: Pure dominance signals are highly primitive. In modern business and relationships, excessive territorial dominance signals often drastically backfire over the long term, eventually leading to deep resentment rather than genuine respect and cooperation.
